newsitem.title: UK: UK's new boy Blair aims to shine on Denver G7 stage.
newsitem.headline: UK's new boy Blair aims to shine on Denver G7 stage.

text.p: He was a hit in Noordwijk at his debut European summit. Europe's centre-left marvelled in Malmo. Will Britain's new prime minister Tony Blair now dazzle the Group of Seven in Denver?

Blair, who has set a cracking pace since his Labour party swept to power in a landslide election victory on May 1, has wasted no time using the authority of his huge 179-seat parliamentary majority to give an international dimension to his domestic policy priorities.

While conscious that preaching to statesmen much more experienced than he could backfire, Blair has not been shy about telling his European Union partners that they need to shake up their ideas to tackle mass unemployment.

"It's not a question of lecturing, but it is a question of saying to people: come on, let's face the common challenges that we have in our countries," he said in Bonn on June 6 after meeting German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.

After years of dealing with a Conservative government that was fundamentally hostile to Europe, Britain's partners have welcomed Blair's promise of a fresh start -- even if they do not share his vision of welfare reform and flexible labour markets.

"Instead of being a helpful junior partner in Kohl's historic project, the Labour premier with the unique mandate is proving a serious competitor in the question of future influence in the Union," the Frankfurter Rundschau newspaper said on the day Blair visited Bonn.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, host of the June 20-22 summit of the Group of Seven industrialised nations in Denver, Colorado, is also a member of the Blair fan club.
The two got on so well when Clinton spent the day in London on May 29 that British newspapers proclaimed the start of a special personal relationship.

Blair seized the moment -- and took a giant stride toward ensuring he can portray Denver as a political success -- by launching a joint initiative with Clinton to put "employability" at the top of the G7 agenda for the next two years.
Britain chairs the G7, which groups Canada, Japan, France and Italy as well as the United States and Germany, in 1998.

In essence, Blair wants to harness the clout of the G7 to bolster his campaign to persuade European leaders to cast aside discredited ideas about the role of the state in order to help the continent's 18 million jobless back to work.
Blair's mantra is more education, skills and training to give people the ability to get a job, plus a Thatcher-style assault on obstacles to companies creating jobs.

"We must be the enablers of enterprise, equipping our people and business to make the most of their talent and ability," he told fellow leaders of Europe'e centre-left parties in Malmo, Sweden, on June 6. They gave him a standing ovation.

In keeping with his successful election strategy of shunning unrealistic goals, Blair has set no numerical targets for his jobs crusade. He says only that he wants progress to have been made by the end of Britain's stint as EU president in mid-1998.
Likewise, he has a relatively modest wish list for Monday's EU summit in Amsterdam, which is due to wrap up a treaty setting out new rules for the bloc and overhauling its institutions.
All the signs are that Blair will get his way at Amsterdam -- giving him another pre-Denver boost -- especially on his core demand that Britain retain control over its external borders.

"We can return from Amsterdam not just having done a good deal for Britain but having obtained a better deal for Britain that the previous government could have hoped to achieve," Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said on Monday.
"We have established Britain as one of the main players in Europe, no longer heckling from the sidelines," Cook added.
Blair, with an 82 percent approval rating after five weeks in office, admits his honeymoon will not last forever.

Some commentators are wondering how long it will take before he falls out with France's new socialist prime minister, Lionel Jospin, whose reliance on the state as the engine for economic growth is at odds with Blair's warm embrace of free markets.

But British officials say more unites Blair and Jospin than divides them. They also note hopefully that the Labour leader has experience, through working with his own deputy John Prescott, of getting left-wing traditionalists to modify their views.
"As a new prime minister he's signalling that he wants a different agenda," a senior British official said. "This is a debate where Blair senses we're ahead of the game."
Denver, and Amsterdam before it, will help show whether that confidence is well-founded.
